newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia Socialists reluctantly accept privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Serbia Socialists reluctantly accept privatisation.

text.p: Serbia's reformists will have to swallow a bitter pill after their proposals to push the country into radical reforms through privatisation suffered major changes, analysts said on Thursday.
Serbia was also seen risking to remain the last communist stronghold in Europe by watering down an initial approach to privatisation seen by some economists as not radical enough.

"The law was sifted through the (Socialist) party filter and came out in a completely different form than the one we have proposed," a member of an expert team entrusted with the first draft privatisation law told Reuters.
"Once again, politics outweighed economic interests of the country. The team will have to swallow a bitter pill," said the source who spoke under condition of annonymity.
Announced by Serbian Privatisation Minister Milan Beko as one of the most important legal documents of the state, the law was hoped to change the ownership picture of Serbia's economy.
After the initial euphoria, the law has undergone many changes with the Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) insisting it is entirely up to companies to decide whether to privatise.
According to Belgrade daily Politika, the SPS main board on Wednesday gave a go ahead to the draft privatisation law.
"The ownership transformation law is one of the fundamental reform documents on which material and spiritual renewal of the society should rest," the SPS main board said.

"The law should allow firms to independently decide whether to privatise and also to be socially fair, meaning that the existing socially-owned and state capital will be distributed to those who created it and not to a small number of people," Politika wrote after the SPS main board met.
The draft privatisation law, first offered to public debate late in March, fell short of voucher privatisation but proposed heavy discounts hoping to motivate companies to launch the process.

Workers, pensioners, farmers and Yugoslavs working abroad, were offerred 14,000 German marks in shares free of charge, but the new version prepared by Socialist hardliners reduces the gift to 6,000 marks.
Also, a total of 20,000 marks eligible for discounts is now heavily reduced. In the latest version, the initial discount of 300 German marks is multiplied by the years of service.
The first draft envisaged discounts running for one year after the law is adopted, but politicians said the discounts will be offered from the day the company enters the process.
The SPS also saw the ownership transformation as a way to partially resolve the problem of frozen hard currency savings by swapping deposits for shares if the depositor agrees to it.
The privatisation law deals only with small and medium companies while the big state firms will be privatised under a special government programme.
Western analysts insisted it was the big state companies making problems to the economy.

"But big loss-makers are unlikely to be privatised, because some government ministers and officials are also company managers and have no interest in privatisation. It is in their interest to delay the process," a Western diplomat said.
Analysts expected privatisation to begin just before Serbian parliamentary and presidential elections due later this year.

"People will be given share certificates just before the elections and that could help the Socialists score another victory," an analyst said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
